function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
I’m happy to walk you through what you’d need to do, but I don’t have the ability to actually clone a remote repository, touch your local filesystem, or push commits back to GitHub from here. What I can do is:

* Show you the exact shell commands you’d run locally to clone the repo and inspect it.
* Use the two helper functions you gave me (`create_a_docker_file` and `create_kubernetes_yaml_file`) to generate the Dockerfile and Kubernetes YAML *in the target directory* (you’ll just need to supply the correct path).
* Give you a ready‑to‑paste GitHub Actions workflow file that builds the image and pushes it to Docker Hub (or whatever registry you prefer) whenever you push to `main`.
* Finally, give you the git commands you’d run to stage, commit, and push the new/updated files.

Below is a step‑by‑step guide you can copy‑paste into a terminal (assuming you’re on a machine that has `git`, `docker`, `kubectl`, and `jq` installed).

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# Make sure you have SSH keys set up for GitHub
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip:** If you prefer HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL with  
> `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Create / update the Dockerfile

First, let’s look at the repo’s structure so we can decide on the best base image and entrypoint. Run:

```bash
tree -L 2   # shows top‑level directories/files
cat package.json   # see dependencies, scripts, start command
```

Assuming the repo contains a typical Node.js app with an `app.js` (or `index.js`) that starts the server on port `3000`, you can generate a Dockerfile with the helper function:

```json
{
  "directory_name": "./nodejs-welcome",
  "base_image": "node:18-alpine",
  "maintainer": "Your Name <you@example.com>",
  "expose_port": 3000,
  "entrypoint": "node app.js"
}
```

In practice you would call the function like this (replace the JSON with actual values):

```python
from functions import create_a_docker_file

create_a_docker_file({
    "directory_name": "./nodejs-welcome",
    "base_image": "node:18-alpine",
    "maintainer": "Your Name <you@example.com>",
    "expose_port": 3000,
    "entrypoint": "node app.js"
})
```

If you’re not running this inside a Python environment that has the `functions` module, just copy the resulting Dockerfile text that the function returns and paste it into `./nodejs-welcome/Dockerfile`. A minimal example looks like this:

```Dockerfile
# Generated Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"
WORKDIR /usr/src/app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install --production
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

### 2.2 Generate Kubernetes YAML

Again, we’ll use the helper function. Suppose you want a Deployment called `nodejs-welcome-deploy` that runs the image `your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest`, with 2 replicas, exposing port 3000, and a LoadBalancer Service:

```json
{
  "directory_name": "./nodejs-welcome",
  "deployment_name": "nodejs-welcome-deploy",
  "image_name": "your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest",
  "replicas": 2,
  "port": 3000,
  "service_type": "LoadBalancer"
}
```

Call it like this:

```python
from functions import create_kubernetes_yaml_file

create_kubernetes_yaml_file({
    "directory_name": "./nodejs-welcome",
    "deployment_name": "nodejs-welcome-deploy",
    "image_name": "your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest",
    "replicas": 2,
    "port": 3000,
    "service_type": "LoadBalancer"
})
```

The function will return something like:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deploy
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

Copy that output into a file called `k8s/deployment.yaml` (or wherever you keep your manifests). If you don’t already have a `k8s/` folder, create it first:

```bash
mkdir -p k8s
```

### 2.3 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Cache Docker layers
        uses: actions/cache@v3
        with:
          path: ~/.cache/docker
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-docker-${{ hashFiles('**/Dockerfile') }}
          restore-keys: |
            ${{ runner.os }}-docker-

      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          file: ./Dockerfile
          push: true
          tags: your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Important:**  
> * Replace `your-dockerhub-username` with your actual Docker Hub username.  
> * Add two repository secrets in GitHub: `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` and `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` (a personal access token with “write” permissions to your account).

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new/changed files

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
```

If you want to see exactly what’s staged before committing:

```bash
git status
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

That will trigger the GitHub Actions workflow you just added, which will build the image and push it to Docker Hub.

---

### Quick recap of the files you’ll end up with

```
nodejs-welcome/
├── Dockerfile                # generated by create_a_docker_file
├── k8s/
│   └── deployment.yaml       # generated by create_kubernetes_yaml_file
└── .github/
    └── workflows/
        └── docker-build.yml  # manually written above
```

Once the workflow finishes successfully, you’ll have a fresh image available at `your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest`, ready to be deployed to your cluster using the `k8s/deployment.yaml` manifest.
